summary: Episode Ten begins with David Choe, Asa Akira, Yoshi Obayashi, Bobby Namba, and Critter in an extended explicit discussion of pornography, anal sex, preparation, hygiene, bodily accidents, fantasy, and what makes a performed scene feel real. The group acknowledges its first audience mail and revisits Lisa Ling's appearance, her sister Laura, North Korea, curiosity, judgment, and the limits of the panel's own speculation. A smaller discussion asks why Yoshi once listened closely to The Clash and The Who but now prefers talk radio. The second half becomes one of the show's defining workplace conflicts. Rody had researched Japanese snacks and brought David chips that David could not replace because he could not enter Japan. The chips disappeared from David's desk; David accused multiple employees, searched the trash, installed or consulted cameras, and considered firing everyone before learning Yoshi had eaten them and treated the mystery as a joke. The room then spends roughly seventy minutes arguing over ownership, gifts, trust, intent, lying, apology, friendship, employer power, and whether the harm comes from the chips, the deception, the accusations, or David's reaction. Asa compares the demanded apology with conflict in her marriage; Bobby and Critter challenge David's behavior; Yoshi apologizes while continuing to explain intent. The episode ends with uneasy reconciliation and Trivia With Bobby on Liam Neeson, Danny Trejo, Sons of Anarchy, and Asa's voice.

connections.label: A trivial object becomes a test of an entire work system
connections.note: The chips matter because they combine Rody's research, David's inability to return to Japan, a gift, a desk boundary, and a workplace where friends are also employees. Treating them as 'just chips' misses why the argument expands; treating every consequence as caused by Yoshi misses David's power over the room.

connections.label: The mystery harms people who never touched the chips
connections.note: David's trust in Yoshi initially redirects suspicion toward Critter, Bobby, Tatiana, and others. Once Yoshi admits eating them, the ethical question is no longer only theft or lying: it includes the accusations, surveillance, anxiety, and threatened firings produced while the truth remained hidden.

connections.label: Intent and impact are repeatedly made to compete
connections.note: Yoshi emphasizes that he did not act maliciously; David emphasizes that the week was still damaged. Asa argues that both can be true. The episode is useful precisely because the attempted apology fails whenever either side treats one of those truths as cancelling the other.

connections.label: A paycheck changes what counts as an equal disagreement
connections.note: David explicitly says friendship remains equal while the boss-employee relationship does not. That distinction clarifies the stakes but also exposes the coercive asymmetry: David can demand an exact apology, dock pay, fire Yoshi, or propose punishment while describing the conflict as interpersonal.

connections.label: Everything can become material, so nothing feels disposable
connections.note: David argues that a wrapper, diary, discarded object, or personal incident may later become a painting, film, book, or podcast. This explains the desk boundary and the archive's breadth, but it cannot by itself communicate consent or ownership rules to the people cleaning and working around him.

connections.label: The cold pancake is the emotional key, not factual proof
connections.note: David's childhood story translates anticipation and sudden loss into a form the room can feel. It explains why the chips activated more than appetite, but it does not prove Yoshi understood that history when he ate them.

connections.label: The episode performs the editorial problem it creates
connections.note: A two-and-a-half-hour unedited dispute supplies multiple incompatible accounts, repeated revisions, jokes, threats, and apologies. A responsible archive must preserve sequence and power rather than compressing it into the fan shorthand 'Yoshi was fired over chips.'

connections.label: The opening's search for 'real' imperfection echoes the later conflict
connections.note: Early discussion values accidents and unscripted reactions as more compelling than polished pornography. The chip dispute produces exactly that authenticity at an interpersonal cost, showing how a no-take-back entertainment format can reward escalation while participants are still inside it.

quality.speaker_state: five-person core plus staff interjections and extensive overlap; named turns withheld
quality.content_note: The episode contains extremely explicit sexual material, pornography and rape-fantasy discussion, racist and homophobic slurs, unsupported cultural claims, bodily waste, medical risk, workplace threats, threatened violence, coercive employer dynamics, privacy concerns, and discussion of deceptive or non-consensual behavior. Editorial framing distinguishes testimony, jokes, unsupported generalization, and independently established fact.

note: Chapter titles and connections are editorial. The existing cleaner is accepted; fifteen correction records and one Rody normalization group should be baked into derived text.
